items.originalTitle: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.summary:
Anthropic redesigned its source control system, creating a custom tool called Scion to manage a dramatic increase in code changes, rising from about 2,500 merges per day in May 2026 to over 30,000 by September. The new system replaced Git to accommodate extreme scale, including a main branch history of nearly 100 GB and 25 million daily code checkouts for continuous integration and other environments.

The migration to Scion was completed in five months by a team of seven engineers. Anthropic also developed a new code review system named Antique and uses adversarial review techniques involving AI models to improve code quality while avoiding over-engineering. The surge in coding activity correlates with the release of new AI models such as Fable and Mythos during 2026, which likely contributed to the increased development velocity.

items.originalSummary:
Redesigning source control at Anthropic

Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.

They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:

This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.

"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements:

The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.

As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:

Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

items.originalTitle: OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room
items.summary:
An OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested and charged with using devices to intercept oral communications after audio recorders were found concealed in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office. Federal prosecutors allege Alfozan, a Saudi national employed since July 2025, installed the devices to capture confidential meetings involving proprietary research and strategic information.

OpenAI discovered the devices in late September and used its AI models to analyze the equipment and its data, then referred the case to the FBI. Surveillance footage and chatbot activity linked to Alfozan and his spouse indicated planning and technical knowledge related to building and encrypting recording devices. The FBI and U.S. attorney's office are prosecuting the case as a national security matter, with Alfozan facing up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine if convicted.

items.originalTitle: I posted to HN, and then my website was flooded with AI bot traffic
items.summary:
A developer who posted about their customizable feed reader on Hacker News experienced a significant increase in AI bot traffic to their website, which caused severe slowdowns. Investigation revealed that nearly half the traffic came from a single service that frequently queried the site to monitor changes and generate AI summaries, alongside other known crawlers and vulnerability scanners.

In response, the developer implemented measures including blocking abusive bots, adding a robots.txt file to manage crawler access, and setting rate limits. They also undertook infrastructure improvements to enhance website performance and scalability, aiming to better handle high traffic volumes in the future.

items.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 embedding model repurposed into a speech-to-text system running on MacBook Air with 5% word error rate [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: We turned EmbeddingGemma 2 into a speech-to-text model
items.summary:
Researchers adapted Google's EmbeddingGemma 2, originally a multimodal embedding model for text, images, audio, and video, into a speech-to-text model that transcribes audio on-device in about 13 seconds per hour of audio on a base MacBook Air. The approach uses the original audio encoder and a small trained reader to map audio slices to text space, selecting the closest word from a large vocabulary and adding punctuation and capitalization with a tiny additional model.

The reader model was trained for under two hours on English speech data, while the base model was not originally designed for transcription. The system achieves a word error rate of about 5%, compared to 2–3% for leading speech models, with plans to improve accuracy through better reader training. Users can transcribe audio files or dictate directly on Mac devices using the Neural Engine, ensuring audio data remains local.

The presentation highlighted the developer's experience starting with a web-based project called mood.site, which helped explore LLM capabilities in coding. They emphasized that while LLMs excel at generating web app code, their effectiveness in game development is limited by the complexity and opacity of game assets and systems. The talk aimed to share these insights more broadly beyond the conference audience.

items.summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.35

I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.)

Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.

Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.

When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.

(I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)

items.title: Rebuilding Companies for the Agentic Era [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Rebuilding Companies for the Agentic Era
items.summary:
Companies have spent the past few years figuring out how to put AI to work. In 2026, some are confronting a bigger question: What should a company look like when AI can understand context, coordinate work and act across systems?

The Information’s Co-Executive Editor Amir Efrati sat down with leaders from three companies at the forefront of this shift to discuss how agentic AI is changing how companies work and operate.

  • Owen Jennings, Business Lead & Executive Officer, Block
  • Stephanie Cohen, Chief Strategy Officer, Cloudflare
  • Surabhi Gupta, CTO, Klaviyo

Redesigning the operating model

Block and Cloudflare offered two ways to rethink the operating model. For Cloudflare, Stephanie Cohen said the company had to rethink the work itself, not simply add AI tools onto existing processes.

“If we didn’t redesign how work was done, we weren’t going to actually change what went on at Cloudflare,” she said. “The only way for us to redesign the factory floor was to get rid of whole functions.”

At Block, the answer was to rebuild its functional model so engineering, product, design and sales teams work across Square, Cash App and Afterpay on shared capabilities. Owen Jennings said the change came about when AI agents became capable of writing production code in complex systems, prompting the company to ask how work should move when agents can share company context with humans.

“We said, based on where the tools are now and based on where we think it’s going, what functions do we need at the company? How do we want to organize?” recalled Jennings.

The shift is showing up in customer experiences, with Square and Cash App surfacing tools, insights or actions at the right moment, rather than relying on static, one-size-fits-all surfaces. Block shipped about three times as many Square features in the first half of 2026 as a year earlier, he said.

“There’s a lot of conversation around automating things for the sake of it,” said Jennings. “For us, it’s about building useful stuff for customers.”

Humans still matter

Companies leaning hardest into agents aren’t necessarily trying to replace humans. Cloudflare hired 1,111 interns this year, including AI-native talent who Cohen said worked on “everything,” including old-fashioned automation no one had made time to build.

“By teaching them the company and allowing them to have access to our system, they’ve shown us a million ways that what we were doing didn’t make sense,” she said.

Block has also built a workspace for working alongside agents. Buzz, an open source tool the company has released for people and AI agents, gives each agent its own identity, permissions and context.

“The idea is not to remove people from the loop, but to make agent work visible and steerable so humans can focus on judgment, taste and customer understanding,” Jennings said.

Klaviyo wants engineers closer to customer outcomes rather than assigned tickets.

“One of the things we’ve found very effective is having the engineers sit side-by-side with the partner functions, and have them become domain experts,” said Klaviyo’s Surabhi Gupta.

Cloudflare runs hands-on workshops that are deliberately low-pressure, and names an AI “champion” on each team, typically someone already experimenting.

“It’s easier to ask a peer than to ask someone else who you feel like is not gonna understand why you don’t know how to do everything,” Cohen said.

Companies also need infrastructure connecting agents to systems, data and context. Cohen described Cloudflare’s approach as a “harness”: a layer connecting AI models with security, systems of record, company context and employee identities, while letting the company switch models as needed.

“Part of the problem is people started with the hammer and were like, ‘here’s this hammer, build this house.’ The reality is you have to design the house,” said Cohen.

The new metrics

Agentic AI is also creating new metrics to measure success. At Block, development velocity—the pace that new features are shipped—has become a key metric. Gupta says Klaviyo measures this too, as well as cost and hours saved as a result of agents.

One metric no one on the panel could predict: headcount, though Cohen felt optimistic about growth.

“My guess is we’ll have more employees [in five years],” she said. “The human world is human-shaped, and humans want to interact with more humans.”

items.originalTitle: Why Companies Can't Prove Their AI Spending Pays Off
items.summary:
The trillion-dollar question of the AI boom is whether businesses’ spending on the technology pays off. But measuring that return is often uncertain, confusing or incomplete. 

That’s because it takes time for AI to show a return on investment that can be demonstrated in a company’s income statement, as we’ve written.

A new study from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School and GBK Collective, a consultancy, echoes this idea, showing that most companies are still tracking ROI by measuring whether it makes their workers more efficient rather than whether it is driving more revenue. The study, based on online surveys of 1,400 U.S.-based employees from firms that have at least 1,000 staff and generate more than $50 million annually, showed that 40% of managers measured AI’s impact on their business in terms of “hours saved per employee” and 37% tracked how AI reduced their workers’ errors. 

Only about 27% of managers said they track the revenue they generate from AI features, apps and tools they provide to their customers.

Perhaps worryingly, 44% of managers said that over the next one to two years, AI’s primary role will be to improve productivity and just 8% said it would be to drive new revenue or create new products.

items.summary:
Neoclouds and so-called inference providers that help app developers run open source models are trying to differentiate themselves in a very crowded market. 

For instance, one such neocloud, Prime Intellect, which was valued at $1 billion in an equity financing in July, is buying a startup to help it make open models run faster and more cheaply on its Nvidia servers, compared to its rivals.  

Prime Intellect, based in San Francisco, is acquiring Moondream, a young developer of open-source models that has fewer than 10 employees, according to Prime Intellect co-founder and CEO Vincent Weisser. (Weisser wouldn’t share the terms of the deal, but Moondream has raised $4.5 million in funding.) 

San Francisco- and Seattle-based Moondream is best known for an open-source vision-language model for analyzing and understanding images, like identifying boxes in an image of a warehouse or ads in a livestream. But Prime Intellect is largely acquiring the startup for its employees’ skills in writing software to make models run more efficiently, Weisser said.

As memory chip makers have quickly expanded manufacturing, companies like Applied and its nearest rival, Lam Research, have enjoyed surging demand for their products.

items.originalTitle: Quoting Geoffrey Huntley
items.summary:
If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten.

— Geoffrey Huntley, nobody should type code by hand anymore. here's what's left.
